title: A planned follow-up for every answer
statement: Plan the follow-up for each kind of answer in advance: challenge a full answer further, hold level on a brief one, and step support down for the rest.
example: One built lesson routes each open answer to one of five paths, and a silent child is taught first, then asked again more easily.
detail: Two sources reach the same branches. A research-based conversation table for early reading scaffolds up on a full answer, holds level on a correct but brief one, and scaffolds down with feedback, reframing, an answer or a model when a child struggles (Zucker et al. 2020). A built Grade 3 lesson's standing dialogue rule routes open answers to full, brief, partial, off-track and silent paths, each of which teaches, and teaches a silent child first before asking again more easily.
against: The research table plans the kinds of move in advance but composes the words in the moment ("Decide the follow-up rule in advance, but compose the follow-up in the moment."), while the built lesson routes each answer to a set path. A later run found: A grade-3 rulebook rules that full credit carries no further ask: a passed answer never shows a push such as 'Make it even stronger' on its find, write-up, short-response, say-back, retell and check surfaces, which bars challenging a full answer further wherever the answer is scored (`grade3-reading/artifacts/judgment-corpus/distilled-src/01-NON-NEGOTIABLES.md`). A later run found counter-evidence (`grade3-reading/artifacts/judgment-corpus/distilled-src/01-NON-NEGOTIABLES.md`).

evidence.quote: When a child answers easily, scaffold up by challenging for reasoning, alternatives, generalizing, or extending. When a child struggles, scaffold down by giving feedback, reframing, supplying an answer, offering a model to mimic, or simply keeping the child engaged (Zucker et al., 2020).
